new_statements.quote: In this study, segmental stress is defined as the prominence (i.e., loudness) of a specific syllable in a given word (Crystal 2008). First, in Bagobo-Klata, segmental stress is contrastive, as shown in Table 11. [Table 11: Contrastive stress in Bagobo-Klata: Penultima [ˈɁuː.la] 'snake' / Ultima [Ɂu.ˈla] 'rain'; [ˈpɔː.tɔj] to 'quarrel' / [pɔ.ˈtɔj] 'to kill' ...] Second, stress is also predictable because of vowel length. Table 12 shows that stress falls on the ultima (i.e., light (CV) or heavy (CVC)) if there is no vowel length. ... On the other hand, Table 13 shows that if a word has vowel length, stress falls on the penultima.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on one of the last two syllables and is lexically contrastive between penult and ultima (minimal pairs like [ˈɁuː.la] 'snake' vs [Ɂu.ˈla] 'rain'). A stressed open penult always carries a long vowel, so the author equivalently states it as: final stress (CV or CVC ultima) when the word has no long vowel, penultimate stress when the penult vowel is long. Vowel length is not set up as an independent phoneme, and the conclusion lists stress (not length) among the contrastive features, hence coded lexical; a weight-sensitive (long-penult-else-final) reading is the same facts under the length-primary analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonology (sec. 7.1, p. 253): the irrealis PV -ɔ, B/LV -a and nominalizing -a delete the antepenult of the affixed form 'while the stress shifts to the penultima' (e.g. ha.ˈwɛt + -ɔ -> ha.ˈwɛː.tɔ -> ˈwɛː.tɔ). CVC ultimas do not attract stress differently from CV (both final-stressed absent length). Antepenultimate stress not attested in the data shown (trisyllables/quadrisyllables in Table 8 are penult- or final-stressed).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms from a 1,026-item elicited wordlist (roots mostly mono/disyllabic); phonetic transcriptions mark primary stress and penult vowel length throughout the paper. No phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bagobo-Klata (endonym Klata; exonym Giangan/Jangan/Guiangan), ISO bgi = Glottolog gian1241, spoken on the eastern slopes of Mt. Apo, Baguio/Calinan/Tugbok districts of Davao City; Estrera and Zorc 2019 both state Giangan and Klata are the same speech community. Data from a 1,026-word list; no dialect differentiation made. Note Glottolog's booktitle for Estrera 2022 ('Studies in the Anthropology of Language in MSEA') is wrong: the paper is in 'Papers from the 30th Conference of SEALS (2021)', JSEALS Special Publication 8, pp. 244-284 (Wikipedia's 283-323 is also wrong).

sources.locator: Section 6 'Segmental Stress', pp. 252-253 (pdf pp. 261-262 of the volume), Tables 11-13; also sec. 7.1 p. 253 and Conclusion p. 266
sources.note: Section 6 'Segmental Stress' (pp. 252-253): stress is contrastive (7 minimal pairs penult vs. ultima, Table 11, penult-stressed member always with a long penult vowel); 'also predictable because of vowel length': ultima (CV or CVC) if no vowel length (Table 12), penultima if the word has vowel length (Table 13). Sec. 7.1: affixes -ɔ/-a delete the antepenult and stress shifts to the penult. Conclusion (p. 266) lists segmental stress among the contrastive features. Vowel length is not listed as a phoneme.
Vowel and consonant inventory only (from Estrera 2022); nothing on stress.
